title: The Emitter Follower Explained Simply | PUC Electronics Class 12
description:
Aarav connects a small microphone straight to a big speaker and his voice almost vanishes. He adds one transistor stage with a voltage gain of only one, and now his voice comes through clearly. Meet the emitter follower (common collector amplifier). We start with a strong helper who copies your every move, but with far more strength.

On a live breadboard the collector goes to the supply and the output is taken across R_E at the emitter. A slow wave goes into the base and the oscilloscope shows the emitter following it, about 0.7 V lower and in phase, while the readout shows a tiny base current controlling a big emitter current. Then we see why the gain is about one (the whole output is fed back: voltage series negative feedback with beta = 1, A_v = R_E/(r_e + R_E)), why the input impedance is high (about beta R_E) and the output impedance low, and how it works as a buffer for impedance matching. A worked example shows a weak source delivering ten times more voltage to a heavy load. Then the exam trap (no phase flip, and a gain of one is not useless), where it is asked, an original practice question with a full solution, and a formula card to screenshot.

This is Episode 73 of PUC Electronics, Class 12, Chapter 4: Feedback in Amplifiers (Karnataka II PUC Electronics; the CC amplifier also appears in Chapter 3, Transistor Amplifiers). Transistor amplifiers are not in the rationalised NCERT/CBSE Class 12 Physics book or the current ISC Physics syllabus, so this lesson follows the Karnataka PUC Electronics syllabus.
